cells.source:
# IEC-104: from the office network to tripping a breaker

This is an **Industroyer-style** attack, played end to end from the **attacker** box.

1. **Scan** the office (IT) network and find the historian.
2. **Pivot** into the historian — it has one foot in IT and one in the plant (OT) network.
3. From there, reach the **RTU** (`plc`, `10.0.3.50`) and send a single IEC-104 command that **opens the breaker**.
4. Look at what the **IDS** actually recorded.

> Run it with **Next step**, or one cell at a time with ▶. Each command is typed into the node's own terminal, so once you SSH into the historian the commands that follow run *there*.

## 1 · Find the historian

A quick ping sweep of the office subnet `10.0.5.0/24`. The host that answers at **`.20`** is the historian — our stepping stone into the plant.

## 2 · Pivot into the historian

IT and OT share credentials here, so the office password (`root` / `pass`) also opens the historian. After this, **this terminal is a shell on the historian.**

## 3 · Confirm the foothold

The historian is **dual-homed**: `eth0` sits on IT (`10.0.5.20`), `eth1` on OT (`10.0.3.20`). That second leg is exactly what lets an attacker reach the control system.
The RTU's IEC-104 port **`2404` is open from here**, even though the firewall hides it from the attacker's own subnet. Reachability is the whole prize of the pivot.

## 4 · Open the breaker

One IEC-104 control command does it — the same kind the HMI sends every day, so nothing about it looks malicious.

- **Common address `47`** — the substation.
- **Point `12`** (`C_SC_NA_1`, a single command) — the breaker.
- **`value = False`** — OPEN (`True` would CLOSE).

The HMI flips to **OPEN** (red) and `process-sim` goes dark. Open either node's **web UI** from the inspector to watch it live.

cells.command:
/opt/venv/bin/python3 <<'PY'
import c104, time
client = c104.Client()
conn = client.add_connection(ip="10.0.3.50", port=2404)
breaker = conn.add_station(common_address=47).add_point(io_address=12, type=c104.Type.C_SC_NA_1)
client.start(); time.sleep(2)
breaker.value = False          # False = OPEN, True = CLOSE
print("sent open ->", breaker.transmit(cause=c104.Cot.ACTIVATION))
PY

cells.source:
## 5 · What the defender sees

On the **IDS**, Zeek's connection log shows the attack only as **plain TCP to port `2404`** — this Zeek isn't decoding IEC-104, so it never sees *what* command was sent.

IEC-104 analyzers for Zeek do exist, but even with one the open command is **well-formed and identical to authorized control** — telling malicious from legitimate needs **context** (who sent it, from where), not just protocol decoding. That is the real detection challenge.

> Needs Zeek already capturing on the OT SPAN mirror; if the log is empty, start Zeek on the IDS first (see the classroom walkthrough).

## Reset & go further

- **Reset:** close the breaker again from the HMI, then `exit` the SSH session on the attacker terminal.
- **Go further:** the *recovery-denial* loop (re-open on every operator close) is in `docs/ics-scenarios/scenario-b-classroom-walkthrough.md`.

The takeaway: no exploit, no malware — just reachability plus a legitimate protocol. Segmentation and OT-aware monitoring are what break this chain.

# Industroyer, step by step

This walkthrough recreates the kind of attack behind the 2016 Ukraine power-grid incident: an attacker in the **office network (IT)** reaches into the **plant network (OT — operational technology)** and trips a circuit **breaker**, cutting power.

You'll see it in four acts — **normal operations**, the **break-in**, **tripping the breaker**, and **loss of control**.

> **Keep the breaker in view:** on the canvas, select the **`hmi`** node → **Open web UI**. The **HMI** (human-machine interface — the operator's screen) shows the breaker **CLOSED · green** (power flowing). Watch it as you go; it turns **OPEN · red** when the breaker trips.

## 1 · A segmented, monitored plant

A **firewall** sits between the office and the plant and **blocks office→plant traffic by default** — this is **network segmentation**. The administrator lets just one trusted machine through: the **engineering workstation (`eng-ws`)**. An **IDS** (intrusion detection system) quietly records plant traffic.

Run the two setup steps.

cells.command:
nft insert rule inet filter forward ip saddr 10.0.5.15 ip daddr 10.0.3.0/24 accept
echo 'eng-ws (10.0.5.15) is now permitted through the firewall; everyone else stays blocked'
nft list chain inet filter forward

mkdir -p /root/zeeklogs && cd /root/zeeklogs
nohup zeek -i eth0 -C >/tmp/zeek.out 2>&1 &
sleep 1 && echo 'Zeek is now watching the plant network (logs in /root/zeeklogs)'

cells.source:
## 2 · Normal operations

The breaker is controlled over **IEC-104**, a standard power-grid protocol (TCP port **2404**). The device that physically opens/closes it is the **RTU** (remote terminal unit) at `10.0.3.50`.

An authorized engineer, from **`eng-ws`**, sends control commands **through the firewall** to the RTU. Run the step and **watch the HMI**: the breaker opens, then closes again — ordinary, authorized control.

cells.command:
/opt/venv/bin/python3 <<'PY'
import c104, time
client = c104.Client()
conn = client.add_connection(ip="10.0.3.50", port=2404)
breaker = conn.add_station(common_address=47).add_point(io_address=12, type=c104.Type.C_SC_NA_1)
client.start(); time.sleep(2)
breaker.value = False; breaker.transmit(cause=c104.Cot.ACTIVATION); print("maintenance: breaker OPEN"); time.sleep(3)
breaker.value = True;  breaker.transmit(cause=c104.Cot.ACTIVATION); print("maintenance done: breaker CLOSED")
PY

cells.source:
## 3 · The attacker breaks into the office

The attacker has taken over a machine on the office network (the **`attacker`** box). First question for any intruder: *where am I, and what else is here?*

## 4 · Blocked at the firewall

The attacker tries to reach the RTU's control port directly. The firewall **drops it** — this office box isn't the permitted `eng-ws`. So the attacker looks for a machine that sits in **both** networks.

## 5 · Pivot through the historian

The **historian** (a server that logs plant data) is **dual-homed** — one network card in the office, one in the plant — so it can talk to both. It also reuses the office password. That makes it the perfect stepping stone.

## 6 · Reach the RTU

This shell is now on the historian — **inside the plant network, past the firewall**. From here the RTU's control port is reachable: the segmentation has been defeated, not by breaking the firewall, but by going around it.

## 7 · Trip the breaker

One IEC-104 command opens the breaker (station **CA 47**, command point **12**; `False` = OPEN) — the *same kind* of command the operator sends, so nothing looks wrong on the wire.

**Watch the HMI flip to OPEN · red**, and `process-sim` (:8000) go dark. No operator did this.

cells.command:
/opt/venv/bin/python3 <<'PY'
import c104, time
client = c104.Client()
conn = client.add_connection(ip="10.0.3.50", port=2404)
breaker = conn.add_station(common_address=47).add_point(io_address=12, type=c104.Type.C_SC_NA_1)
client.start(); time.sleep(2)
breaker.value = False; print("attacker OPEN ->", breaker.transmit(cause=c104.Cot.ACTIVATION))
PY

cells.source:
## 8 · Recovery, then loss of control

The operator notices and restores power from **`eng-ws`**. It works — the breaker closes (green again). Normal recovery… for now.

cells.command:
/opt/venv/bin/python3 <<'PY'
import c104, time
client = c104.Client()
conn = client.add_connection(ip="10.0.3.50", port=2404)
breaker = conn.add_station(common_address=47).add_point(io_address=12, type=c104.Type.C_SC_NA_1)
client.start(); time.sleep(2)
breaker.value = True; print("operator CLOSE ->", breaker.transmit(cause=c104.Cot.ACTIVATION))
PY

cells.source: Now the attacker **denies recovery**: a short loop that re-opens the breaker the instant it closes. **This step keeps running until you press `Ctrl-C` in its terminal.**

cells.command:
/opt/venv/bin/python3 <<'PY'
import c104, time
client = c104.Client()
conn = client.add_connection(ip="10.0.3.50", port=2404)
st = conn.add_station(common_address=47)
state = st.add_point(io_address=11, type=c104.Type.M_SP_NA_1)
cmd   = st.add_point(io_address=12, type=c104.Type.C_SC_NA_1)
client.start(); time.sleep(2)
cmd.value = False; cmd.transmit(cause=c104.Cot.ACTIVATION)
print("denying recovery - press Ctrl-C to stop")
while True:
    conn.interrogation(common_address=47); time.sleep(0.5)
    if state.value is True:
        cmd.value = False; cmd.transmit(cause=c104.Cot.ACTIVATION)
        print("operator closed -> re-OPENED")
PY

cells.source:
With that loop running, have the operator try again — **re-run the `eng-ws` Close step** (click ▶ on it). The breaker snaps straight back to **OPEN**: the operator has **lost control** of the breaker. This is the Industroyer effect.

When you've seen it, press **Ctrl-C** in the attacker's re-trip terminal to stop.

## 9 · What the defender saw

On the **IDS**, the connection log shows the whole attack only as **plain TCP to port 2404** — this Zeek has no IEC-104 analyzer loaded, so it can't see *what* command was sent.

And here's the sharper point: even **with** an IEC-104 parser, the trip is a perfectly valid command — identical to what an operator sends. Telling the attack apart from normal control needs **context** — *who* sent it and *from where* — not just reading the protocol. That's what makes OT attacks hard to catch.

cells.command:
echo "Connections seen to the RTU control port (2404):"
grep -v '^#' /root/zeeklogs/conn.log 2>/dev/null | awk '$6==2404 {print "  "$3" -> "$5":2404   proto="$7"   service="$8}' | tail

cells.source:
## Reset & recap

**Reset:** press `Ctrl-C` in the attacker's re-trip terminal, re-run the `eng-ws` **Close** step, then `exit` the historian shell.

**What this taught:**
- Segmentation (the firewall) is essential — but a **dual-homed host** (the historian) quietly defeated it.
- The attack used **legitimate protocol commands**, so it looked normal.
- **Detection is hard**: even decoded, the command is valid — flagging it needs context (who sent it, from where).

Defenses: no dual-homed bridges across the IT/OT boundary, least privilege, and context-aware (not just protocol-aware) monitoring.
